commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether restricting staff to approved tools, banning PHI in public tools, defining permitted prompt data, or privacy training reduces PHI exposure. Six surveys and query-log analyses show that clinicians and students enter patient data into unapproved tools at rates that range from under 3% to 48.6% across groups.

perspectives.view: No study tests the recommended controls, so certainty about their effect is rated as no direct evidence. The six hazard studies are cross-sectional surveys or query-log analyses that rely mostly on self-report. Their estimates range from under 3% of physical therapy professionals entering identifiable data to 48.6% of hematologists entering patient data, which suggests inconsistency across professions and countries.

Among French student users, 23.5% reported at least one disclosure of patient-identifying information, and 8.2% of Turkish hematologists entered identifiable data. Another 47.1% of student users processed real medical content they perceived as anonymized, which may indicate that users misjudge what counts as identifiable and that training would need to address this.

In an analysis of 106,942 physician queries, 2.68% contained sensitive information, mostly from writing and editing tasks. Among medical students using ChatGPT, 21.0% used it to help write clinical notes. These findings suggest that rules on permitted prompt data and approved tools would need to cover documentation and editing workflows.

Among 78 French oncology pharmacists, 65.3% reported using unsanctioned AI and 62.5% reported concern about patient data confidentiality. This pattern suggests that staff demand exists and that a ban without approved alternatives may not change behavior. No supplied study reports the cost or staffing needed to put these controls in place.

Endorsing sources, including the CHAI playbooks, call for defining which clinical data may enter prompts and for HIPAA- or GDPR-compliant platforms procured under institutional agreements. No supplied study examines whether these policies improve compliance with privacy law, so support for the recommendation rests on existing privacy obligations and expert consensus.

None of the six hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations or the staff who serve them. The studies come from the United States, Türkiye, France, and one unreported setting, so the rate of PHI exposure in safety-net care is unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares PHI exposure before and after an organization adopts approved-tool restrictions, prompt data rules, or privacy training. Controlled or interrupted time-series studies that measure disclosure objectively, for example through audited prompt logs rather than self-report, would show whether these controls reduce exposure and whether staff move to unsanctioned tools in response.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and none of the six hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups have no evidence on how often PHI exposure occurs in their settings or whether these controls would work there, and training materials may need separate testing for staff and patients with differing language and literacy needs.
